body.head: The Departing Soul's Address to the Body: A Fragment of a Semi-Saxon Poem / Discovered Among the Archives of Worcester Cathedral

div.head: The Departing Soul's Address to the Body: A Fragment of a Semi-Saxon Poem / Discovered Among the Archives of Worcester Cathedral
DISCOVERED AMONG THE ARCHIVES OF WORCESTER CATHEDRAL,

LONDON:
PRINTED BY LUKE JAMES HANSARD & CO.

p.hi: The student of our early literature and language is indebted to the zeal of Sir Thomas Phillipps, for the discovery of the following interesting Fragment, which appears to have formed part of a volume that contained Ælfric's Grammar and Glossary, probably of the Twelfth Century. The fragments were discovered among the archives of Worcester Cathedral; and in 1836 Sir Thomas Phillipps printed the whole of them in folio. I know not whether the form or the typographical arrangement has been the cause of the neglect of this publication; but it has escaped both Mr. Wright and Mr. Thorpe. The former, in his interesting edition of "The Latin Poems of Walter de Mapes," where he has given the literary history of this legend with extracts, has not even referred to our fragment; nor has Mr. Thorpe adverted to it in his publication of the "Codex Exoniensis," which contains an Anglo-Saxon poem of the same kind, with which it is interesting to compare this later version of the legend. There is a portion of another semi-Saxon poem, entitled "The Grave," printed in Mr. Conybeare's "Illustrations," and by Mr. Thorpe in his "Analecta Anglo-Saxonica," which appears to be by the same hand, or at any rate of the same school and age. Indeed some of the lines and thoughts are identical with passages of the following poem. Mr. Thorpe has justly called "The Grave" a singularly impressive and almost appalling fragment; expressions equally characteristic of that with which the reader is here presented.

This impressive character, coupled with the interest which the fragment possesses, as a specimen of the moral poetry of our ancestors, and as throwing light upon the transition of our language from Saxon to English, has been the motive for producing it in a more legible form than that in which it first appeared.

In one of the smaller poems (No. V.), printed by Mr. Wright with the Owl and the Nightingale, from the Cottonian MS. Calig. A. ix. "The sorie sowle maketh hire mone," in language not dissimilar to that used in the following fragment; and the dreary imagery of the house appointed for all living, and the punishment which awaits a wicked life at its close, are painted in an equally fearful manner.

Mr. Thorpe points to an Anglo-Saxon prose Homily as the original of the poem on the same theme in the Exeter MS., which is repeated, with some variation, in the Vercelli Codex. In a rude and simple age this dramatic way of awakening the sinner to a sense of his perilous state, was perhaps the most effective that could have been chosen, and it was naturally a favorite with the moral and religious teachers for some centuries. M. Karajan, in a very pleasing little publication (Frülingsgabe für freunde Alterer Literatur, Wien 1839) has printed the "Visio Philiberti," a Latin poem in dialogue on this subject, with two old German versions; and the notes contain some interesting information relating to similar compositions; but Mr. Wright's volume, before referred to, contains ample illustrations of the legend in all languages.

The fragment here given, it will be seen, is very defective. An attempt has been made to supply words which were wanting, from the mutilation of the MS. leaves; but what is engrafted on the original is scrupulously distinguished by the Italic character. A version has also been added, the imperfections of which those who are acquainted with the difficulties of such renderings will best know how to excuse.

The language of this poem seems to have a striking resemblance to that of one of the MSS. of Laȝamon, and we may hope, when the lovers of our early lore shall be favoured with the long and anxiously expected edition of that work by Sir Frederick Madden, that much light will be thrown upon the history of the transitions of our language.

For what has been already done by Conybeare, Price, Kemble, Thorpe, Madden, Stevenson, Wright, Way and others, the present writer is most grateful; but he would wish to see the same spirit and enthusiasm, the same unwearied zeal displayed in the elucidation of the noble remains of our Anglo-Saxon ancestors, and of the interesting stores of our early literature and language, which has been so long a distinguishing feature of Germany, whose example has of late years lighted up a similar patriotic flame in France and Belgium.

div.head: DEPARTING SOUL'S ADDRESS TO THE BODY.
div.p: but there is a sad portion
hit woaneth and mænet theo weowe.
it waileth, and bemoans the woe,
that shall the soul from her body
thonne the licame and the sowle.
when the body and the soul
it is of kin to him.
mon hine met mit on ȝerde.
They measure him with a yard,
ne mot he of thære molde.
nor will they, with their hands,
binds up the mouth of the dead,
for ufel is that wrecche lufe.
for evil is that wretched love

p.hi: why wouldst thou not think of me

div.p: theo hwule thet ic wunede inne the.
while that I dwelt in thee,
for thu were leas and lutiȝ.
for thou wert false and deceitful,
Where are now the vessels of gold
as they came to thy hands?
thin blisse is nu al igon.
Thy bliss is now all gone;
that help might come to thee?
They thought it all too long
nu heo hi dælith heom imang.
Now they divide it among them,
to bringen the ut of huse.
to bring thee out of house;
bergen the ut æt thire dure.
bearing thee out at the door.
Why wouldst thou not think of me
theo hwile ic was innen the.
give them part of thy wealth
that they might pray for thee,
that they might with psalm sung
that he shed on the cross,
and soth hit is on boken.
in books, and true it is:
eart thu nu loth and unwurth.
Thou art now loathsome and contemptible
Now they think it all too long
theo swetnesse is nu al agon.
The sweetness is now all gone,
that swete ne cumeth the næffre.
that sweet cometh to thee never.
sæ ne thearft thu on stirope.
see, thou canst not on stirrup
for thu scalt faren alto howe.
for thou shalt journey all to woe,
nu mon mæi seggen bi the.
Now they may say of thee,
and his weolæn beoth her belæfed.
and his wealth is here left behind.
nolde he nefre thær of don.
nor hast thou but well away!
Thou wouldst not in thy house
ne mihten heo under thine roue.
nor might they under thy roof
ac thu sete on thine benche.
but thou sate on thy bench,
Now thou hast a new house,
thin rof liith on thin breoste ful nei.
thy roof lieth on thy breast full nigh.
for they think all too little
thou thoughtest that it thine were.
heo wulleth freten thin fule hold.
they will devour thy foul carcase,
as long as they find it;
that hoard is open to them,
for love, give of thy goods;)
nu me wule swopen thine flor.
Now men will sweep thy floor,
for it is the loather to them
al hit is reowliche thin sith.
nes hit the no wiht icunde.
it was no whit known to thee
it was not known to thee
more then thine cunne biuoren the.
more than to thy kin before thee,
ne heold is thin æiȝe opene.
nor was thine eye held open
theo hwule ic the inne was.
Now they dwell in the earth,
and mid worde and mid werke.
for thin wombe was thin god.
for thy belly was thy god,
forloren thu havest theo ece blisse.
thou hast deprived thee of Paradise.
binumen the is that holi lond.
Taken from thee is that holy land;
then deofle thu bist isold on hond.
thou art given into the devil's hand,
for noldest thu nefre habben inouh.
for thou wouldst never have enough,
Nu is that swete al agon.
Now is the sweet all gone,
thet gode ne cumeth the nefre.
that good cometh to thee never.
that he would not take thee,
for thou ever raised up strife
and ic was with innen the.
for the deofle lored the all.
for the devil taught thee all,
ær thu to hire to cume.
that were so pleasant to thee;
it was hateful to the Lord.
and now thou art in his power;
ne bith he ne mare undon.
nor will it be ever opened
ær cume thæs heiȝe kinges dom.

div.p: thu * * * et drowe me to the.
well away! and woe is me!
that ic efre com to the.
that I ever came to thee;
for noldest thu mid thine muthe.
for thou wouldst not with thy mouth
ther alle men secheth ham ore.
ac ne the scalt nefre resten.
thou wouldst not with thy mouth
thou art laid out with rags,
and loath to all thy friends,
he is thick set with quills;
for the soft part is all
ac thu al that softe was.
but thou all that was soft
thus it all came to pass:
ac hit is nu all igon.
but it is now all gone
that were hateful to the Lord.
It is said in the Psalm,
and ful sothe hit is bihire.
and full true it is of her:
thauh ic thonne that sothe repie.
though I then the truth gathered,
but thou didst hinder that fostering.
that he would have given me.
Thou hadst the mark of royalty;
thou mightst have been in heaven,
if thou hadst not forfeited it
as I was given to thee
